_comment: Explain It (Merit tier). Stage 1: click hotspot and pick 'principle_choices'. If correct, stage 2 offers 'explanation_choices' - each has a 'tier' (merit/achievement/not_achieved) and 'feedback'. Exactly one choice per question should be tier 'merit' (the genuinely correct answer, linked to the interface's purpose); one should be tier 'achievement' (a true but surface-level description of the principle - correct fact, but doesn't link it to the purpose); the rest are tier 'not_achieved' distractors, at least one of which should test a commonly confused principle pair.

questions.prompt: TrailFoot Outdoors wants customers to complete their purchase confidently. Click the step tracker, then explain why it matters.
questions.interface_purpose: help customers complete a purchase without giving up partway through

explanation_choices.text: It shows the customer exactly how many steps are left, which reduces the chance they'll abandon the purchase out of uncertainty - directly supporting the checkout's purpose.
explanation_choices.feedback: That's it - you've linked the feature to why it matters for the customer completing their purchase, not just what it is.

explanation_choices.text: It shows the current step out of four steps in the checkout process.
explanation_choices.feedback: True, but that just restates what the feature does. Merit needs you to link it to why it helps the customer finish their purchase.

explanation_choices.text: It stops the customer from entering an invalid delivery address.
explanation_choices.feedback: That would be Error Prevention, not Visibility of System Status - the step tracker doesn't stop mistakes, it shows progress.

explanation_choices.text: It lets the customer undo their last action if they change their mind.
explanation_choices.feedback: That would be User Control and Freedom. A progress tracker doesn't give an escape route, it just shows where the customer is.

questions.prompt: CityBus Live lets a passenger cancel a ticket purchase at any point. Click the cancel option and explain why it matters.
questions.interface_purpose: let passengers buy tickets quickly without feeling trapped in the process

explanation_choices.text: It gives a passenger who changes their mind mid-purchase a clear way out, so they're not forced through to payment against their wishes - which keeps the app trustworthy.
explanation_choices.feedback: Exactly - you've explained why the escape route matters for the passenger's trust in the app, not just named the button.

explanation_choices.text: There is a 'Cancel and exit' button on the screen.
explanation_choices.feedback: That's accurate, but it just describes the button. Merit needs the WHY, not just the WHAT.

explanation_choices.text: It lets an expert passenger buy tickets faster using a shortcut.
explanation_choices.feedback: That's the common mix-up: an emergency exit (User Control and Freedom) is not the same as a shortcut for experienced users (Flexibility and Efficiency of Use).

explanation_choices.text: It shows the passenger which route they have selected.
explanation_choices.feedback: That's describing a different part of the screen, not the cancel option, and doesn't relate to this principle.

questions.prompt: Kōrero Cloud is a community forum. Experienced members can press a key combination to post instantly. Click the shortcut hint and explain why it matters.
questions.interface_purpose: let both new and experienced members post comfortably

explanation_choices.text: It lets members who already know the forum post in one keystroke, saving them time, while new members can still just click Post - so the interface serves both groups without slowing anyone down.
explanation_choices.feedback: Right - you've connected the shortcut to speeding up experienced use without removing the option beginners already understand.

explanation_choices.text: There is a keyboard shortcut, Ctrl+Enter, that posts the comment.
explanation_choices.feedback: Correct fact, but it's just naming the shortcut. Merit needs you to explain why offering it (alongside the normal button) helps both kinds of users.

explanation_choices.text: It gives the member a way to undo their post if they change their mind.
explanation_choices.feedback: That would be User Control and Freedom - an escape route. A keyboard shortcut for posting faster is a different idea: Flexibility and Efficiency of Use.

explanation_choices.text: It reduces how much text the member has to read on screen.
explanation_choices.feedback: That's closer to Aesthetic and Minimalist Design and doesn't explain what the shortcut itself is for.

questions.prompt: TrailFoot Outdoors asks for confirmation before deleting a saved address. Click the confirmation dialog and explain why it matters.
questions.interface_purpose: stop customers from losing information they didn't mean to delete

elements.text: This can't be undone. 123 Fern Street will be permanently removed.

explanation_choices.text: It stops an accidental tap from permanently deleting the address before any damage is done, matching how serious and irreversible the action is.
explanation_choices.feedback: Yes - you've linked the confirmation step to stopping the mistake before it happens, matched to how serious it is.

explanation_choices.text: There is a message asking the customer to confirm before deleting.
explanation_choices.feedback: That's true but only describes the dialog. Merit needs you to explain why catching the mistake beforehand matters here.

explanation_choices.text: It tells the customer what went wrong and how to fix it after the address was deleted.
explanation_choices.feedback: That describes Error Recovery, which happens after a mistake. This confirmation appears before the delete happens - that's Error Prevention.

explanation_choices.text: It provides a help article about managing saved addresses.
explanation_choices.feedback: There's no help article shown here - that would be Help and Documentation, a different feature entirely.
